title: Why Zooming Cannot Split Two Dots

scenes.tts: Here is a puzzle. Two vesicles, each filled with G F P, sit one hundred fifty nanometres apart. In the best ordinary light microscope, they look like one blob. Zoom in, and the blob only gets bigger. Why can you not split them? The reason is a property of light.
scenes.caption: Here is a puzzle. Two vesicles, each filled with GFP, sit 150 nanometres apart. In the best ordinary light microscope, they look like one blob. Zoom in, and the blob only gets bigger. Why can you not split them? The reason is a property of light.
scenes.visual: Two green vesicles 150 nm apart go through a microscope and come out as one red-labelled blob; zooming only enlarges the blob.
scenes.narration: Here is a puzzle. Two vesicles, each filled with GFP, sit 150 nanometres apart. In the best ordinary light microscope, they look like one blob. Zoom in, and the blob only gets bigger. Why can you not split them? The reason is a property of light.

scenes.tts: Think of a rubber stamp with a soft, round face. However small the point you aim at, the mark is the size of the stamp. A lens does the same thing to light. The image of one point is a bright disc with faint rings. That is called an Airy pattern. Two marks closer than about one stamp width run together.
scenes.visual: A stamp presses a tiny point and leaves a big mark; the stamp becomes a lens that turns a point into a disc with rings; two marks slide together and merge.
scenes.narration: Think of a rubber stamp with a soft, round face. However small the point you aim at, the mark is the size of the stamp. A lens does the same thing to light. The image of one point is a bright disc with faint rings. That is called an Airy pattern. Two marks closer than about one stamp width run together.

scenes.tts: Two glowing points give two patterns, and their intensities add. We call the points resolved when the centre of one pattern falls on the first dark ring of the other. That spacing is the resolution. It depends on the emission wavelength, and on the numerical aperture. The numerical aperture measures how wide a cone of light the lens gathers.

That spacing is the resolution. It depends on the emission wavelength, and on the numerical aperture (NA). The numerical aperture measures how wide a cone of light the lens gathers.
scenes.visual: Two intensity curves add; the second is slid until its centre sits on the first's first dark ring; that spacing d is marked; wavelength and a lens cone (NA) are named.
scenes.narration: Two glowing points give two patterns, and their intensities add. We call the points resolved when the centre of one pattern falls on the first dark ring of the other. That spacing is the resolution. It depends on the emission wavelength, and on the numerical aperture (NA). The numerical aperture measures how wide a cone of light the lens gathers.

scenes.tts: Take light of five hundred twenty nanometres, like the glow of G F P. Use an oil lens with a numerical aperture of one point four. The resolution is zero point six one, times five twenty, divided by one point four. That is two hundred twenty-six point six nanometres. A weaker lens, with a numerical aperture of one, gives three hundred seventeen point two. Losing a little aperture costs about ninety nanometres.
scenes.caption: Take light of 520 nanometres, like the glow of GFP. Use an oil lens with a numerical aperture of 1.40. The resolution is 0.61 times 520, divided by 1.40. That is 226.6 nanometres. A weaker lens, with a numerical aperture of 1.00, gives 317.2. Losing a little aperture costs about 90 nanometres.
scenes.visual: The worked sum builds line by line while the single-point curve shows its first dark ring at 226.6 nm; at NA 1.00 the curve widens and the ring moves out to 317.2 nm.
scenes.narration: Take light of 520 nanometres, like the glow of GFP. Use an oil lens with a numerical aperture of 1.40. The resolution is 0.61 times 520, divided by 1.40. That is 226.6 nanometres. scenes.tts: Now put the vesicles back. They are one hundred fifty nanometres apart, closer than two hundred twenty-six point six. Their two blurs overlap and add into one spot. That single merged spot is all the camera records. Enlarge the picture, and the spot spreads over more screen pixels. It adds no new information.
scenes.caption: Now put the vesicles back. They are 150 nanometres apart, closer than 226.6. Their two blurs overlap and add into one spot. That single merged spot is all the camera records. Enlarge the picture, and the spot spreads over more screen pixels. It adds no new information.
scenes.visual: Two blurs 75 nm either side of centre add into one hump; 150 nm bracket is shorter than the 226.6 nm bracket; the pixel bars are enlarged and stay one hump.

scenes.tts: Super-resolution gets around the limit by controlling which molecules glow. Switch on a sparse few at a time, so that no two neighbours glow together. The centre of each blur can be found far more precisely than the blur is wide. Plot the positions from thousands of cycles. Locating one molecule is not the same as resolving two. Because neighbours glow at different times, molecules closer than the limit can be told apart. Remember the rule. Magnification without resolution is empty magnification.
